title: Been vs gone: someone away
question: 'Tom has ___ to Brazil. He won't be back until Friday.' Which is correct?
explanation: Use 'gone' with 'has' when someone is away now. 'Been' would mean Tom has already returned, 'went' is past simple and cannot follow 'has', and 'going' is not a past participle.

title: Been vs gone: someone returned
question: 'I've ___ to Brazil twice. It's a beautiful country.' Which is correct?
explanation: Use 'been' (past participle of 'be') with 'have' for a completed visit. 'Went' and 'was' are past simple and cannot follow 'have', and 'being' is an -ing form.

title: Been vs gone: question form
question: 'I'm back home now. I've just ___ to the dentist.' Which is correct?
explanation: 'Been' means you went and have come back. 'Gone' would mean you are still away, 'went' is past simple and cannot follow 'have', and 'going' is not a past participle.

title: For vs since: duration
question: 'We've lived here ___ fifteen years.' Which is correct?
explanation: 'Since fifteen years', 'from fifteen years', and 'ago fifteen years' are all ungrammatical with present perfect duration. Use 'for' with a period of time.

title: For vs since: point in time
question: 'She's worked at the bank ___ she graduated.' Which is correct?
explanation: 'For she graduated', 'from she graduated', and 'ago she graduated' are ungrammatical. Use 'since' with a point in time or past event.

title: For vs since: tricky duration
question: 'I haven't eaten anything ___ this morning.' Which is correct?
explanation: 'For this morning', 'from this morning', and 'ago this morning' are ungrammatical with present perfect. 'This morning' is a point in time, so use 'since'.

title: For vs since: tricky period
question: 'He's been ill ___ a long time.' Which is correct?
explanation: 'Since a long time', 'from a long time', and 'ago a long time' are ungrammatical. 'A long time' is a duration, so use 'for'.

title: Still/already/yet: negative still
question: 'She ___ replied to my message, even though I sent it hours ago.' Which is correct?
explanation: 'Still' goes before 'hasn't' to show surprise at an ongoing absence. 'Hasn't still', 'yet hasn't', and 'already hasn't' are all ungrammatical word orders.

title: Still/already/yet: already in statements
question: 'You are quick! You have ___ finished the whole book.' Which is correct?
explanation: 'Already' goes before the past participle and shows something happened sooner than expected. 'Yet' is for negatives and questions, 'ever' asks about experience and 'ago' goes after a time period.

title: Still/already/yet: yet vs still
question: 'I haven't decided ___.' Which is correct?
explanation: 'Yet' goes at the end of a negative present perfect sentence and means 'up to now': 'I haven't decided yet.' 'Already', 'still' and 'ever' do not fit after the verb here.

title: Present perfect vs past simple: finished time
question: 'I ___ three cups of coffee yesterday morning.' Which is correct?
explanation: 'Yesterday morning' is a finished past time, so use past simple 'had'. 'Have had' and 'has had' are present perfect, and 'am having' is present continuous.

title: Present perfect vs past simple: unfinished time
question: Which sentence is correct?
correct: I have had two meetings this week.
wrong1: I have had two meetings last week.
wrong2: I has had two meetings this week.
wrong3: I have two meetings had this week.
explanation: 'This week' is unfinished, so present perfect 'have had' is right. 'Last week' is a finished time and needs past simple; 'has' does not agree with 'I'; the participle must follow 'have'.

title: Present perfect vs past simple: unfinished today
question: 'I ___ three strange emails so far today.' Which is correct?
explanation: With 'so far today', use present perfect: 'have received'. 'Has' does not agree with 'I', 'receive' is not a past participle, and 'am receiving' is present continuous.

title: Present perfect: already
question: 'Don't worry about dinner -- I ___ already eaten.' Which is correct?
explanation: Use present perfect 'have eaten' for a recent completed action with present relevance. 'Did', 'am' and 'was' cannot be followed by 'already eaten'.

title: Present perfect vs past simple: result now
question: 'I can't find my keys. I ___ them.' Which is correct?
explanation: 'Has lost' does not agree with 'I'; 'lose' and 'will lost' are wrong forms. Present perfect 'have lost' shows a past action with a present result.

title: Present perfect vs past simple: question with a past time
question: 'What time ___ you get home last night?' Which is correct?
explanation: Use past simple 'did' in questions about a finished time like 'last night': 'What time did you get home?'

title: Present perfect vs past simple: no time word
question: '___ you seen my phone anywhere?' Which is correct?
explanation: With the past participle 'seen', use present perfect: 'Have you seen...?' 'Did', 'are' and 'do' cannot be followed by 'you seen'.

title: Present perfect: lifetime experience
question: Which sentence is correct?
correct: We have been to Paris twice in our lives.
wrong1: We have been to Paris twice last year.
wrong2: We has been to Paris twice in our lives.
wrong3: We were been to Paris twice in our lives.
explanation: Present perfect describes life experience up to now: 'have been'. 'Last year' is a finished time and needs past simple, 'has' does not agree with 'we', and 'were been' is not a tense.

title: Polite request: could
question: '___ you pass me the salt, please?' Which is correct?
explanation: 'Could you' is a standard polite request form. 'Does', 'is' and 'were' cannot be followed by 'you pass'.

title: Can vs could: past ability
question: 'When I was young, I ___ run very fast.' Which is correct?
explanation: Use 'could' for ability in the past: 'When I was young, I could run fast.' 'Can', 'must' and 'may' do not fit a finished past time.

title: Could: present possibility
question: 'I'm not sure where Anna is. She ___ be at the library.' Which is correct?
explanation: 'Could' expresses uncertain possibility: 'She could be at the library.' 'Mustn't' and 'needn't' do not express possibility, and 'ought' needs 'to'.

title: Must vs have to: obligation form
question: 'I really ___ study harder.' Which is correct?
explanation: 'Must' is a modal. It takes the bare verb, with no 'to' and no 'am' or 'do' before it: 'I must study harder.'

title: Must vs have to: past obligation
question: 'Yesterday I ___ wait an hour for the bus.' Which is correct?
explanation: 'Must' has no past form, so use 'had to' for past obligation. 'Must', 'have to' and 'can' do not fit 'yesterday'.

title: Don't have to: no necessity
question: 'You ___ shout; I can hear you perfectly well.' Which is correct?
explanation: The negative of 'have to' meaning 'not necessary' is 'don't have to'. 'Don't must', 'haven't to' and 'not have to' are not English.

title: Mustn't: prohibition
question: 'You ___ touch that wire. It's dangerous!' Which is correct?
explanation: 'Mustn't' expresses prohibition and is followed by the bare verb: 'You mustn't touch it.' No 'to', no 'don't' before a modal.

title: Modal form: may
question: 'Excuse me, ___ I come in? Sorry I'm late.' Which is correct?
explanation: 'May I...?' is a polite way to ask permission. 'Am', 'does' and 'are' cannot be followed by 'I come'.

title: Might: possibility form
question: She isn't here. Maybe she ___ have missed the bus. Which is correct?
explanation: 'Might' is a modal for possibility and is followed by the bare infinitive 'have'. 'Did', 'was' and 'is' cannot be followed by 'have missed' here.

title: Must: logical deduction
question: 'He's been working for 12 hours. He ___ exhausted.' Which is correct?
explanation: Use 'must' for a strong deduction: after 12 hours of work he 'must be' exhausted. 'Can't be' would say it is impossible, and 'must is' and 'must being' are ungrammatical.

title: Should: advice form
question: 'You look tired. You ___ go to bed early tonight.' Which is correct?
explanation: 'Should' gives advice and is followed by the bare verb: 'You should go.' 'Ought' needs 'to', and 'should to' and 'must to' add an extra 'to'.

title: Can't: logical impossibility
question: 'That ___ right. The math doesn't add up.' Which is correct?
explanation: Use 'can't be' for a logical impossibility: the sum is wrong, so it can't be right. 'Must be' would say it is certainly right, and the others are ungrammatical.

title: Going to: prediction form
question: 'She's driving far too fast. She ___ crash!' Which is correct?
explanation: 'Is going' is missing 'to'; 'going to' is missing the auxiliary 'is'; 'is go to' is ungrammatical. The full form is 'is going to' + bare infinitive.

title: Will: spontaneous decision form
question: 'The phone is ringing. I ___ answer it.' Which is correct?
explanation: 'Will' is used for decisions made at the moment of speaking: 'I will answer it.' 'Going to' needs 'am', and 'am going' needs 'to' before the verb.

title: Going to: planned intention form
question: 'We ___ visit Grandma this weekend. We arranged it yesterday.' Which is correct?
explanation: 'Are go to' is ungrammatical; 'is going to' doesn't agree with 'we'; 'are going' is missing 'to' before the infinitive. The full form is 'are going to visit'.

title: Going to: evidence-based form
question: 'Look! That tree is shaking. It ___ fall down!' Which is correct?
explanation: 'Is going' is missing 'to'; 'going to' is missing 'is'; 'are going to' doesn't agree with 'it'. The correct form is 'is going to' + bare infinitive.

title: Will: negative form
question: 'Don't ask him -- he ___ help you. He's in a bad mood.' Which is correct?
explanation: The negative of 'will' is 'won't' (will not). 'Isn't', 'hasn't' and 'haven't' cannot be followed by the bare verb 'help'.

title: Going to: negative form
question: 'I ___ going to eat that -- it smells strange.' Which is correct?
explanation: The negative of 'am going to' is 'am not going to'. 'Aren't' does not agree with 'I' in a statement, and 'don't' and 'not am' are not used with 'going to'.

title: Will: form with promise
question: 'I ___ help you with your homework after dinner.' Which is correct?
explanation: 'Will' is a modal followed by the bare verb: 'I will help.' It takes no 'am' or 'do' before it and no 'to' after it.

title: Will: question form
question: '___ you be home before ten tonight?' Which is correct?
explanation: Form will-questions with 'Will + subject + base verb': 'Will you be home?' 'Do', 'does' and 'have' cannot be followed by 'you be home'.

title: Present perfect: ever in questions
question: '___ she ever eaten octopus?' Which is correct?
explanation: With 'she' and the past participle 'eaten', use 'Has': 'Has she ever eaten...?' 'Have' does not agree with 'she', and 'did' and 'does' cannot be followed by 'eaten'.

title: Going to: intention form
question: 'I ___ learn to drive this summer. I've already booked lessons.' Which is correct?
explanation: 'Am go to' is ungrammatical; 'going to' is missing the auxiliary 'am'; 'am going' is missing 'to' before the bare infinitive 'learn'.

title: Question tag: positive to negative
question: 'You've been to London, ___?' Which is correct?
explanation: 'Haven't I' doesn't match the subject 'you'; 'don't you' uses the wrong auxiliary; 'hasn't you' has wrong agreement. Use 'haven't you' after 'you've'.

title: Question tag: negative to positive
question: 'She doesn't like coffee, ___?' Which is correct?
explanation: After a negative statement, use a positive tag with the same auxiliary: 'doesn't like' gives 'does she?' The other auxiliaries do not match the verb.

title: Question tag: with will
question: 'They'll come to the party, ___?' Which is correct?
explanation: After a positive statement with 'will', use a negative tag with the same modal: 'They'll come, won't they?' The other auxiliaries do not match 'will'.

title: Question tag: with can't
question: 'You can't swim, ___?' Which is correct?
explanation: After a negative statement, use a positive tag with the same modal: 'can't swim' gives 'can you?' The other auxiliaries do not match 'can't'.

title: Question tag: imperative
question: 'Close the door, ___?' Which is correct?
explanation: For imperatives, use 'will you' as the tag: 'Close the door, will you?' 'Do', 'are' and 'have' do not fit an imperative.

title: Question tag: nobody
question: 'Nobody called, ___?' Which is correct?
explanation: 'Nobody' is negative, so the tag is positive, with 'did' to match 'called': 'Nobody called, did they?' 'Didn't they' repeats the negative, and 'do' and 'were' do not match 'called'.

title: Question tag: somebody
question: 'Somebody left their bag here, ___?' Which is correct?
explanation: After a positive statement, use a negative tag with the same auxiliary: 'left' gives 'didn't they?' 'Did they' is positive, and 'don't' and 'haven't' do not match 'left'.

title: Question tag: I am
question: 'I'm right, ___?' Which is correct?
explanation: The fixed tag for 'I am' is 'aren't I'. 'Don't I' and 'isn't I' use the wrong auxiliary, and 'am I' would be a positive tag after a positive statement.

title: Question tag: let's
question: 'Let's go for a walk, ___?' Which is correct?
explanation: The fixed tag for 'let's' is 'shall we'. 'Will', 'do' and 'aren't' are not used after 'let's'.

title: Present perfect: past participle of 'take'
question: 'She has ___ the dog for a walk.' Which is correct?
explanation: The past participle of 'take' is 'taken' (irregular). 'Took' is past simple and cannot follow 'has'; 'taked' is not a word; 'taking' is a present participle.
